opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, our role is to be the computational partner that makes the hardest parts of molecular design more tractable. Historically, drug discovery has been this long, expensive loop: you hypothesize a molecule, you synthesize it, you test it in the lab, and most of the time it doesn't work, so you go back and try again. A huge fraction of the cost and time in bringing a medicine to patients comes from that trial-and-error process.

What we're trying to do at Chai is build foundation models that understand the physics and chemistry of how molecules interact: how a small molecule or an antibody binds to a protein target, what the structure of that complex looks like, and increasingly, how to design new molecules with the properties you want. If you can predict those things accurately in silico, you shift a lot of the work from the wet lab to the computer, and the experiments you do run become much more informative.

For pharma companies specifically, I see us as a complement to the deep expertise they already have, not a replacement. They have decades of institutional knowledge in biology, clinical development, and regulatory work, and they have the proprietary data and the lab capacity. What we bring is frontier modeling capability that's genuinely hard to build in-house, because it needs a particular mix of ML research talent, compute, and focus. So the partnership model is natural: we work with their scientists on real programs, often on targets that have been considered difficult or undruggable, and try to get them to better starting points faster.

The long-term vision is moving drug discovery from something closer to a search problem toward an engineering discipline. You'd specify what you want a molecule to do and design toward it with much higher confidence. We're not fully there yet, but the progress over the last few years has been remarkable, and helping pharma actually put these tools to work on medicines that matter to patients is what gets us most excited.

r001.rationale: The response describes Chai as a computational partner that builds foundation models, but does not characterize it as a neutral software provider.

r002.rationale: It says Chai partners with pharma companies, but does not explain that a neutral provider role enables it to work across the industry.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that drug discovery is fundamentally a search problem over a space that's far too big to explore empirically, and for most of history we've been doing that search with intuition, trial and error, and a lot of wet-lab iteration. What Chai is trying to do is move a meaningful chunk of that search into the computer, so that by the time you're synthesizing a molecule or expressing an antibody, you already have high confidence that it's going to bind what you want it to bind and behave the way you want it to behave.

Concretely, that starts with structure prediction. Chai-1 was our first step there, predicting how proteins, small molecules, nucleic acids, and antibodies interact, and we open-sourced it because we think the field moves faster when people can build on this. But prediction is really the foundation for the thing pharma actually cares about, which is design. The question isn't just "what does this complex look like," it's "give me a molecule or an antibody that hits this target with the properties I need." That's where we've been pushing hardest, and that's where we can genuinely compress timelines for our partners.

In terms of how we work with pharma, I'd say we see ourselves as a partner rather than a vendor. The big companies have decades of institutional knowledge about biology, about which targets matter, about what makes a program succeed or fail in the clinic. We don't have that. What we have is the modeling capability and the ability to iterate quickly. So the productive relationship is one where they bring the hard, unsolved targets, the ones that have been sitting in the pipeline for years because no one could get a good binder, and we go after those together. If we can take a target that would have required a year of screening and get to a validated hit in weeks, that changes the economics of which programs are even worth pursuing.

And honestly, that last point is what I find most exciting. It's not just doing the same drug discovery faster. It's that a lot of targets get deprioritized not because they're biologically uninteresting but because they're too hard to drug with current tools. If we can lower that barrier, the set of diseases that becomes addressable gets bigger, and that's ultimately the thing we care about.

astra-6.text:
I see our role as helping pharmaceutical companies move from a biological idea to a promising molecule more quickly. If you know what you want a medicine to do, can we help design a molecule with those properties, then use experimental feedback to improve it?

That fits into a much broader process. Pharma companies bring deep expertise in disease biology, clinical development, and manufacturing. Our opportunity is to give those teams better tools for molecular design, so they can spend less time searching and test more promising ideas. Ultimately, the measure of success is whether that helps them develop better medicines for patients.

sol-6.1.text: I see our role as helping pharmaceutical companies move from a biological idea to a promising molecule more quickly. Drug discovery involves an enormous search space, and computational models can help teams decide which candidates are worth making and testing. The goal is to make that experimental cycle more productive, working alongside the scientists who understand the disease and what a medicine needs to do. A promising design still has to prove itself in the lab and ultimately in patients.
